analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants for government searches of Americans' communications and bars police from buying personal data from brokers.
analysis.headline: Four senators from both parties introduced the Government Surveillance Reform Act in March 2026, but the bill has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote since the day it was referred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federal agencies to get a court warrant before searching communications collected under Section 702 of FISA about Americans, and would apply similar warrant rules to surveillance conducted outside FISA altogether. It also bans federal law enforcement from buying Americans' location, browsing, and other personal data from data brokers, requires warrants for phone location and email records, and adds judges' advocates and retention limits to the surveillance courts. At the same time, it extends Section 702 itself, the program that collects foreigners' communications, through April 2030.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone living in the United States. The bill would end warrantless government searches of Americans' calls, texts, emails, and web history collected under Section 702, stop police from buying location and personal data from brokers to dodge warrant requirements, and extend the same protections to surveillance done under executive orders rather than FISA. People whose data ends up in government databases would also get a five-year retention limit and limits on using that data against them in criminal, civil, and administrative cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone whose calls and data are collected

how_it_helps.text: Requires a court order or warrant before any federal employee can access Americans' communications collected under Section 702, closing the 'warrantless query' loophole with narrow exceptions for emergencies, consent, and defensive cybersecurity.

Bans federal law enforcement agencies from buying personal data — including location and biometric information — from data brokers, and blocks them from getting the same data indirectly through other agencies, with evidence obtained that way inadmissible in court.
Prohibits 'reverse targeting' — using surveillance of foreigners as a pretext to collect a specific American's communications — and makes a primary foreign-intelligence purpose a legal requirement.
Requires warrants for location information, web browsing and search records, and email under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, and protects car data from federal warrantless searches.
Applies warrant, retention, and query limits to surveillance conducted for foreign intelligence purposes outside FISA, such as under executive orders, closing the main loophole around the new rules.

Adds court-supervised limits on demands for help from phone and internet providers, repeals the expanded definition of which companies can be forced to assist surveillance, and destroys collected data about Americans that is not foreign intelligence after five years.

Expands the civil-liberties and technical advocates who must be appointed to argue before the secret FISA court, requires written records of the Justice Department's communications with that court, and mandates declassification and accuracy checks in surveillance applications.

analysis.who_pays: The intelligence community and federal law enforcement give up tools: no more warrantless searches of Section 702 data about Americans, no more buying broker data to circumvent warrants, and extra court steps before demanding assistance from phone and internet companies. Data brokers lose federal law enforcement as a customer base. National security officials have long argued warrant requirements slow counterintelligence and counterterrorism work; that trade is the bill's core cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Intelligence agencies, federal police, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill extends Section 702 — the collection program it reforms — through April 20, 2030, so critics who want the program to lapse outright would see it entrenched for four more years even as warrant rules tighten.

The warrant requirement for queries carries exceptions — imminent-threat emergencies, person consent, and defensive cybersecurity — and emergency accesses are reviewed only after the fact, with reports to the court and Congress due 14 days later.

The data broker ban leaves openings: agencies may still buy data mixed into larger compilations if they minimize afterward, and data sold with a sworn attestation that it is 'lawfully obtained public data' is exempt, a process that relies on broker honesty.

Intelligence and law enforcement officials have long argued that requiring individual warrants for 702 queries would slow urgent counterintelligence and counterterrorism work — the central good-faith objection the bill asks Congress to accept in exchange for privacy protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are broad and concrete: warrant protection for Americans' communications, an end to police buying location data to skip warrants, and real court and advocate oversight of a secret court. The cost is real friction for intelligence work, and the bill's answer to Section 702's approaching expiration is to reauthorize it through 2030 rather than let it lapse — a compromise that will disappoint opponents of the program on one side and warrant-requirement opponents on the other. The broker-purchase ban's attestation and compilation exceptions are weaker than a flat ban. On balance the bill trades four more years of a controversial collection program for the strongest warrant and accountability protections that coalition could agree on.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill in March 2026 and it was referred the same day to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the Government Surveillance Reform Act of 2026 on March 12, 2026, joined from the start by Senators Mike Lee, Elizabeth Warren, and Cynthia Lummis — a bipartisan pairing of privacy critics from both parties.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced; the public record shows no further action of any kind.

The timing matters: Section 702, the collection program the bill would reform and extend, is set to expire in April 2026 under the two-year extension enacted in the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act, and this bill would push that expiration to April 20, 2030.

The bill is an updated version of a Government Surveillance Reform Act that previous coalitions of privacy advocates pushed in prior Congresses; like those predecessors, it has so far not been brought to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the intelligence community and federal law enforcement keep the status quo — including warrantless querying authority as it stands — and data brokers keep selling to the government, while the 702 reauthorization fight proceeds without this bill as the vehicle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies and data brokers, for now

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and has been Congress's leading advocate for Section 702 warrant requirements

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan cover from the right

for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill a second Republican backer

against.name: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction day and has taken no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crosses party lines — two Republicans and one Democrat joined the Democratic sponsor — but no one has opposed the bill on the record yet, so the opposition shape is unknown.

industries.note: The Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act title bars federal law enforcement from buying Americans' personal, location, and biometric data from brokers and closes the workaround of getting it through other agencies. Brokers have built a market selling to police exactly what a warrant would otherwise be needed to obtain, so this cuts off a customer base.

industries.industry: Intelligence community and federal law enforcement
industries.note: Agencies would lose warrantless access to Section 702 data about Americans, indirect broker purchases, and surveillance-by-executive-order workarounds, while facing retention limits, records requirements, and accountability procedures. In exchange, the bill hands them a four-year reauthorization of 702 through 2030, which is why the bill is a compromise rather than a shutdown of the program.

The bill subjects technical-assistance demands to FISA Court approval with necessity and undue-burden findings, and voids past directives to entities no longer defined as providers, easing the burden of being conscripted into government surveillance. Providers' interest here runs alongside their customers' privacy.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is in session until January 3, 2027, and Section 702's April 2026 expiration makes reauthorization a live vehicle: this bill is positioned as the reform-and-extend alternative. But with no Judiciary Committee action months after referral, the realistic path mirrors prior surveillance reform bills — it stalls unless Wyden's coalition attaches warrant conditions to a must-pass 702 extension on the floor, and absent that it dies quietly at the end of the Congress.
